opus-5.5.text:
I think the agent paradigm forces us to rethink architecture from the inference side first, rather than treating inference as an afterthought of pre-training.

In the chatbot era, a typical interaction was short: a question, maybe a few turns, then an answer. With agents, a single task can run for hundreds of steps. The model calls tools, reads the results, writes code, runs it, sees errors, and tries again. So the context keeps growing, often to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, and most of those tokens are tool outputs and intermediate states, not human language. That changes what "efficient" means.

The first implication is long-context efficiency. If attention cost and KV cache grow linearly or worse with every step, an agent becomes very expensive and slow. That's why things like sparse attention, hybrid architectures that mix linear attention with full attention, and aggressive KV cache compression become essential rather than optional. You have to design for the case where the model holds a huge working memory at a reasonable cost.

The second is decoding speed. An agent is fundamentally a loop, and latency compounds across every step. A model that is slightly smarter but twice as slow per token may actually be worse for agentic tasks, because the user waits for the whole trajectory. So inference throughput, multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, and how well the architecture fits the hardware all become first-class design goals.

The third, which I find most interesting, is that architecture and training can't be separated anymore. Agent capability mostly comes from reinforcement learning on long trajectories, and RL is dominated by rollout cost. If your architecture is expensive to sample from, you can't afford enough RL, and you won't get a strong agent. So when you choose an architecture, you're really choosing how much RL you can do later. In that sense, inference efficiency is training efficiency.

There's also a question of what the model should remember versus what it should look up. Agents interact with an environment, so not everything needs to live in the parameters. That might push us toward models that are very good at reasoning and using context, and slightly less obsessed with memorizing everything.

So my short answer is that the agent paradigm shifts the center of gravity. We used to ask how to make pre-training as efficient as possible. Now we have to ask how to make long, interactive, multi-step inference cheap enough that we can both train on it with RL and serve it to people at scale. Architecture design should start from that question.

r001.rationale: The response says RL rollout cost depends on inference efficiency, but does not state that agent post-training compute may equal pretraining compute.

r002.rationale: The response discusses designing architectures around inference and RL, but does not say that prolonged post-training can make architecture assumptions obsolete by the time it finishes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that we used to design architectures for a single forward pass, and now we have to design them for a long-running process.

In the chat era, the unit of work was one question and one answer. You optimized for how good that answer was, maybe how fast it came back. Context was something the user gave you, and it was mostly short. With agents, the unit of work becomes a trajectory: dozens or hundreds of steps, tool calls, observations coming back that the model didn't write, intermediate state that has to survive for a long time. So almost every assumption underneath the architecture gets stressed in a new way.

The first and most obvious one is context. An agent's context is not a document, it's a working memory that keeps growing, and most of what's in it is noise relative to the current step. So attention cost and context length stop being a benchmark number and become the thing that decides whether the system is even viable economically. That pushes you toward designs where the cost of the long tail of context is much lower than full attention, and toward thinking about what the model should actually keep versus compress or externalize. I think we'll see architectures where memory is a first-class component rather than something you bolt on with a retrieval system afterwards.

The second is that inference and training stop being separable in the way they were. For an agent, most of the useful signal comes from running the thing in an environment and seeing what works. So the architecture has to be cheap to roll out, not just cheap to serve. Things like inference efficiency, KV cache size, how well the model handles long generations with lots of tool interruptions, these directly determine how much reinforcement learning you can afford. A model that's slightly stronger per token but twice as expensive to sample can actually end up weaker as an agent, because you got half the training signal.

The third thing, which I think people underestimate, is robustness to inputs the model didn't choose. In a chat, the model mostly sees text written by people. In an agent loop, it sees compiler errors, half-broken JSON, truncated logs, outputs from other models. The distribution is much messier. And an error early in a trajectory compounds. So you care a lot more about things like whether the model can recover, whether it can notice it's drifting, whether it can hold a plan steady over a long horizon. Some of that is training, but some of it is architectural: how reasoning is interleaved with action, how much the model can revise its own earlier state.

And then there's the question of specialization. I don't think the answer is one giant model doing everything in one context. Agent systems naturally decompose: a planner, workers, verifiers. So you start thinking about the model less as a monolith and more as a family of components that need to be trained to work with each other, and the architecture question becomes partly a systems question.

If I had to compress it: the chat era optimized the model for the quality of a single output, and the agent era forces you to optimize it for the economics and stability of a long process. That's a different objective, and I think it will end up producing visibly different architectures, not just the same transformer with a longer context window.

r001.rationale: The response says agent training benefits from affordable rollouts, but does not state that post-training compute may equal pretraining compute.

r002.rationale: It says agent workloads stress existing architectural assumptions, but does not say prolonged post-training makes those assumptions obsolete by the time training finishes.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that we need to design for a model that acts over time, rather than one that produces a single answer. An agent takes an action, observes what happened, and decides what to do next. So the architecture has to support that whole loop.

For example, context becomes more than a question of how many tokens you can fit. The model needs to retain useful information, update its understanding when new evidence arrives, and avoid carrying irrelevant details through every step. That makes memory and state management much more central.

There’s also a different compute tradeoff. If an agent makes many model calls to finish a task, the cost and latency of each call compound. You want it to spend more computation on difficult decisions and less on routine steps. That creates a stronger motivation for architectures that can allocate computation adaptively.

But I wouldn’t assume that agents necessarily require a completely new backbone. Some of these capabilities can live in the surrounding system. The important research question is which ones should be learned inside the model and which should remain explicit tools or external memory. We should judge those choices by whether the agent can reliably complete a task, recover from mistakes, and do so efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adaptive computation and the cost of repeated agent calls, but it does not state that agent-model post-training compute may equal pretraining compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss prolonged post-training or say that it could make architecture-design assumptions obsolete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the agent paradigm changes the unit we’re designing for. Before, we mostly thought about a model receiving a prompt and generating an answer. With an agent, the model participates in a loop: it observes, reasons, takes an action, receives feedback, and decides what to do next. So we need to optimize for the whole loop, not just a single response.

That puts more pressure on memory and state. What should stay in the context window? What should be stored externally? And how does the model retrieve the information it needs without repeatedly processing everything? Simply making the context window longer doesn’t solve all of those problems.

It also changes how we think about computation. Some decisions are very simple; others require planning, tool use, or checking an earlier result. Ideally, the system should spend computation according to the difficulty of the decision.

But I would distinguish the model architecture from the architecture of the agent system. You can build a lot of this around an existing model. The interesting research question is which capabilities benefit from being learned inside the model, and which should remain explicit components outside it. I don’t think the agent paradigm automatically implies replacing the Transformer. It does mean that we should evaluate architectural choices by how well they support reliable action over many steps.

r001.rationale: The response discusses allocating computation based on decision difficulty, but does not state that agent-model post-training compute may equal pretraining compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prolonged post-training or explain that it could make architecture-design assumptions obsolete.
